## Libraries

```{r}
library(bayesrules)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggpubr)
library(plotly)
library(report)
```

## Intro

Welcome to today's lecture, we will analyze Capital Bikeshare Data from Washington D.C.

```{r}
bikes_data <- bayesrules::bikes
```

### Starter Questions:

1.  What is the distribution of ridership? Make a histogram and write what you see below

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x=rides)) + 
  geom_histogram(color = "black") + 
  theme_bw()
```

2.  Has ridership increased over time? Make a plot and write what you see below

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x=rides, fill = month)) + 
  geom_histogram(color = "black") + 
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
line_plot <- ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x=date, y = rides, label = day_of_week)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point()
ggplotly(line_plot)
```

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = as.factor(year), fill = as.factor(year), y = rides)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  geom_jitter()
```

3.  Are there more rides on weekdays or weekends? Make a plot and write what you see below

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = weekend, fill = weekend, y = rides)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  geom_jitter()
```

4.  Does temperature feel effect ridership?

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = temp_feel, y = rides)) + 
  geom_point()
```

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = temp_feel, y = rides)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  stat_cor()
```

What is a correlation coefficient and p value: [helpful tool here](https://rpsychologist.com/correlation/)

R = 0.58 — the strength and direction of the pattern you're looking at

- On the -1-to-1 scale, 0.58 sits in moderate territory: real and clearly visible in the scatter, but the cloud of points still has meaningful width around the line, not tightly hugging it the way an R of 0.9+ would.

Squaring it tells you something more concrete about the plot: R² ≈ 0.34

- About 34% of the vertical scatter in ridership across this plot is explained by where a point sits on the x-axis (temperature). The remaining 66% is everything else the plot doesn't capture.

p \< 2.2×10⁻¹⁶ — how confident you should be that this pattern is real, not a fluke of these particular 500 days

- This tests the hypothesis that temperature and ridership have no linear relationship at all in the underlying population, and this pattern is just coincidental noise from sampling 500 particular days. The p-value says: if that null hypothesis were actually true, seeing a correlation as strong as 0.58 in a sample this size would be astronomically unlikely.

```{r}
lm(data = bikes_data, rides~temp_feel)
```

`(Intercept)` = -2179.27: the model's predicted ridership when temp_feel = 0. As flagged before, this is a real number the formula produces, but not a practically meaningful one — 0°F essentially never happens in D.C., so this is just "where the line would cross the y-axis if you extended it that far," not a usable prediction.

`temp_feel` = 81.88: the slope — for every one-unit (one degree) increase in temp_feel, the model predicts ridership increases by 81.88 rides. This is the number that actually answers "does temperature matter, and by how much."

```{r}
model <- lm(rides ~ temp_feel, data = bikes_data)
report(model)
```

## Your turn

Repeat all the steps to model the relationship between:

### Rides and humidity

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = humidity, y = rides)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  stat_cor()
```

*Read off the plot: R and p in the top corner tell you the strength/direction and significance. Square R to get R² — the % of scatter in rides explained by humidity.*

```{r}
model_humidity <- lm(rides ~ humidity, data = bikes_data)
model_humidity
report(model_humidity)
```

*Interpretation template: the slope tells you the predicted change in rides for a one-unit increase in humidity — note the sign, since humidity often correlates negatively with ridership (unlike temperature).*

### Rides and windspeed

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = windspeed, y = rides)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  stat_cor()
```

```{r}
model_windspeed <- lm(rides ~ windspeed, data = bikes_data)
model_windspeed
report(model_windspeed)
```

*Interpretation template: check whether the R value is noticeably weaker than temp_feel's 0.58 — windspeed tends to have a smaller, sometimes negative, effect on ridership.*

### Rides and temp_actual

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = temp_actual, y = rides)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  stat_cor()
```

```{r}
model_temp_actual <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual, data = bikes_data)
model_temp_actual
report(model_temp_actual)
```

*Interpretation template: compare this R/slope to temp_feel's. Since temp_actual and temp_feel are closely related measurements of the same thing, expect a similar (though not identical) relationship with rides.*

### temp_feel and temp_actual

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = temp_actual, y = temp_feel)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  stat_cor()
```

```{r}
model_temp_compare <- lm(temp_feel ~ temp_actual, data = bikes_data)
model_temp_compare
report(model_temp_compare)
```

*Interpretation template: this one isn't about ridership at all — it's checking how closely "feels like" temperature tracks actual temperature. Expect a very high R here (likely well above 0.9), since temp_feel is derived largely from temp_actual plus factors like humidity and windspeed.*
